Nineteen comments

La Partida

La Partida is a venezualan waltz which I heard at a contra dance once and it quickly became a favorite of mine. After endless searching, I found it in Peter Barnes’ compelation “A Little Couple-Dancemusik”.

It works wonderfully with flamenco-style guitar accompaniment and is relly much easier to dance to than it is to transcribe.

↳ Posted by Jack Sparow on September 21st, 2004.

Oops

As I alluded to in my first comment, this tune was very difficult for me to tanscribe and there were some mistakes that I didn’t correct before the sheetmusic and sound file went up. I have now fixed them all (I think) in the ABC section.

“La Partida” - the low down for the limitation of winds

Here are some other possibilities if your limit is D below the treble staff. The eight bars given for the A-part can also be used as an alternate for the last eight bar conclusion of the B-part, or pick it up as given when the low notes are usually reached, the last 5 bars…

La Partida, X:7

This is how I learned it from my former bandmate, Kitty Greenwood – I don’t remember where she got it from.

It sits very well on the fiddle and mandolin in A minor – and, on the mandolin, at least, it is easy to play in the next octave up (using the open E-string as a pedal) or to add a high harmony on the 1st part.

La Partida, X:8

This is what I got from listening to Dominique Riviere ( accordian ) linked on this page.
I have transposed it to Am ( on flute ) to avoid the prominent and awkward C#s / E pattern in the first part.
I first got this tune from Mary Staunton’s “Circle of Friends” CD
I also like | ~B3 edc | for a variation in bar 6 in the A part.

Re: La Partida

The Venezuelan composer Carlos Bon(n)et (1892-1983) began his musical career in an Army band in 1904. He held several important positions as conductor and won a competition to write a march or hymn for his country’s Air Force. Radio, and later television, developped in parrallel to aviation in the 1930’s and el maestro Bonnet wrote several marches for Radio Caracas (RCR & RCTV). I do not know whether those first official hymns are still aired today.
